variants.title: Size the service
variants.context: Capacity is the maximum work a system can handle per unit of time. Assume requests are evenly distributed and every server sustains its stated rate.
variants.prompt: Traffic is 250 requests/second. Each server handles 100 requests/second. What is the minimum whole number of servers?
variants.hint: Divide traffic by capacity per server, then round up.
variants.explanation: 250 / 100 = 2.5, rounded up to 3, because rounding down leaves requests with nowhere to go.

mistakes.feedback: Two servers provide 200 requests/second, below the required 250.
You cannot run half a server; round the result up.

variants.title: Size the service
variants.context: Capacity is the maximum work a system can handle per unit of time. Assume requests are evenly distributed and every server sustains its stated rate.
variants.prompt: Traffic is 730 requests/second. Each server handles 200 requests/second. What is the minimum whole number of servers?
variants.hint: Divide traffic by capacity per server, then round up.
variants.explanation: 730 / 200 = 3.65, rounded up to 4, because rounding down leaves requests with nowhere to go.

mistakes.feedback: Three servers provide 600 requests/second, below the required 730.
Round the quotient up to a whole server.

variants.title: Size the service
variants.context: Capacity is the maximum work a system can handle per unit of time. Assume requests are evenly distributed and every server sustains its stated rate.
variants.prompt: Traffic is 1250 requests/second. Each server handles 300 requests/second. What is the minimum whole number of servers?
variants.hint: Divide traffic by capacity per server, then round up.
variants.explanation: 1250 / 300 = 4.17, rounded up to 5, because rounding down leaves requests with nowhere to go.

mistakes.feedback: Four servers provide 1200 requests/second, below the required 1250.
Round the quotient up to a whole server.

variants.title: Plan for one failure
variants.context: Failure headroom is spare capacity that keeps the service working when a component fails. Assume the load balancer immediately redistributes traffic to the survivors.
variants.prompt: You must still serve 250 requests/second at 100 per server after ONE server fails. How many servers must run before the failure?
variants.hint: Work out how many must survive, then add the one that may fail.
variants.explanation: Three servers must survive, plus one that may fail, so four run normally.

mistakes.feedback: After a failure only two remain, and they serve just 200 requests/second.
Three survivors are enough, so one spare covers the single failure.

variants.title: Find the actual bottleneck
variants.context: A bottleneck is the component whose capacity limits the whole request path. Adding capacity elsewhere does not remove that constraint.
variants.prompt: Application servers handle 250 requests/second but the database serves only 120 reads/second, and every request reads once. What happens if you double only the application servers?
options: Each database read becomes twice as fast.
optionFeedback: Application capacity does not change how fast a read completes.
The shared database is still the limiting component here.
Requests queue on the same database as before.
variants.hint: Each request still needs the same database read.
variants.explanation: A path is bounded by its slowest required component, so measure that component before scaling another one.

variants.title: Find the actual bottleneck
variants.context: A bottleneck is the component whose capacity limits the whole request path. Adding capacity elsewhere does not remove that constraint.
variants.prompt: Application servers handle 730 requests/second but the database serves only 300 reads/second. You add a cache that serves 60% of reads. What is the new ceiling?
options: Still about 300 requests/second, because the database itself has not changed.
About 730 requests/second, because the application servers become the new limit.
About 750 requests/second, because 300 database reads now cover more traffic.
optionFeedback: Most requests are now served by the cache and never reach the database.
The database stops being the constraint, and the next component takes over.
That ignores the application servers, which cannot exceed 730 requests/second.
variants.hint: Work out the traffic 300 database reads can support, then check the other component.
variants.explanation: 300 misses at a 40% miss rate would allow about 750 requests/second, but the application servers cap the path at 730, so the bottleneck has moved rather than disappeared.

variants.title: Find the actual bottleneck
variants.context: A bottleneck is the component whose capacity limits the whole request path. Adding capacity elsewhere does not remove that constraint.
variants.prompt: Application servers handle 1250 requests/second but the database serves only 450 reads/second. The team proposes a faster load balancer. What will that achieve?
options: Nothing, because the database is the limiting component.
It doubles throughput by spreading the load more evenly.
It removes the need to measure database capacity at all.
optionFeedback: The requests still queue behind the same 450 reads per second.
Even distribution does not create database capacity.
The limiting component still has to be measured.
variants.hint: Which component is every request waiting on?
variants.explanation: Adding capacity away from the bottleneck spends money without moving the ceiling.
